1,3-Enynes with Malonates and CO
2

ABSTRACT: Difunctionalization of unsaturated carbon−carbon
bonds with carbon dioxide (CO
2
) provides expedient access to
functionalized carboxylic acids. Compared to the well-developed
carboxylation of alkenes or alkynes with CO
2
, the catalytic
carboxylation of 1,3-enynes has remained unknown. Herein, we report the first visible-light-promoted 1,4-carbon/carboxylation
of 1,3-enynes with malonates and CO
2
, leading to a series of valuable tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoic acids with high efficiency. This
new methodology features good functional group compatibility, ease of scale-up, and facile transformations. Mechanistic
investigations indicate that successive single-electron transfer (SSET) reduction is involved to generate the key allenoic anion
intermediate.
A
llenes are important structural motifs found in various
natural products, bioactive pharmaceuticals, as well as
functional molecules, such as lcariside, kumausellene, (+)-scor-
odonim, and (−)-panacene (Figure 1).
1
They can also serve as
valuable intermediates and catalysts/ligands for a range of
organic transformations.
2
Among them, 2,3-allenoic acids are
of particular interest owing to their versatile reactivities,
3
such
as the Morita−Baylis−Hillman reactions,
3d−f
rearrange-
ments,
3g
cyclization reactions,
3h−j
and other transformations.
Consequently, substantial efforts have been devoted to their
synthesis.
4
Conventionally, allenoic acids could be synthesized
via the Wittig reaction of ketenes with phosphorus ylides
followed by hydrolysis, although this method suffered from a
poor atom economy (Scheme 1a).
5
Recently, transition-metal-
catalyzed functionalization of propargylic alcohols and their
derivatives emerged as a practical method for the synthesis of
2,3-allenoates.
6
For example, Ma and co-workers pioneered an
elegant palladium-catalyzed coupling reaction of 3-alkoxycar-
bonyl propargylic carbonates and boronic acids toward diverse
tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoates (Scheme 1b).
7
Furthermore,
transition-metal-catalyzed carbonylation of propargylic alcohol
derivatives, using CO as the carbonyl source, provides an
alternative efficient route to 2,3-allenoic acids (Scheme 1c).
8
Alternatively, organocatalytic nucleophilic addition of various
nucleophiles to electron-deficient 1,3-conjugated enynes can

9
Despite these great achievements, the develop-
ment of additional robust approaches for convenient access to
2,3-allenoic acids from readily available materials remains in
high demand.
Carbon dioxide (CO
2
) has emerged as an environmentally
benign and renewable C1 feedstock in the synthesis of various
value-added fine chemicals, owing to its natural abundance,
cost-effectiveness, and low toxicity.
10
Among the diverse CO
2
transformations, the carboxylation reactions stand as one of the
most convenient routes toward carboxylic acids.
11
In this field,
carboxylation of unsaturated hydrocarbons with CO
2
is most
attractive, as it avoids the use of halides or moisture-sensitive
organometallic reagents.
12
For example, Martin and co-
workers,
13
Yu and co-workers,
14
Wu and co-workers,
15
Xi
and co-workers,
16
and we
17
have developed a series of practical
visible-light-driven carboxylation reactions of alkenes with
CO
2
, enabling the synthesis of diverse functionalized and
structurally tunable aliphatic carboxylic acids through judicious
selection of radical precursors. Furthermore, transition-metal-
catalyzed or base-promoted difunctionalization of alkynes with
CO
2
also represents an effective route to furnish diverse acrylic
acids.
18
For example, Wu and co-workers reported a novel
route for the synthesis of lactones or acrylic acids by iridium/
cobalt co-catalyzed hydro- or carbocarboxylation of alkynes
with CO
2
.
19
Additionally, Hong and Zhan independently
reported the visible-light-promoted α-aminoalkyl- or phospho-
no-carboxylation of allenes with CO
2
, leading to a series of β-
functionalized allylic carboxylic acids with good efficiency.
20
However, to the best of our knowledge, the carboxylation of
1,3-enynes with CO
2
remains unreported to date. In view of
the high value of allenoic acids and in continuation of our
interest in the CO
2
chemistry,
21
we envisioned the photo-
catalytic carboxylation of 1,3-enynes with malonates and CO
2
,
leading to allenoic acids in one step (Scheme 1d).
Initially, (3-methylbut-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)benzene 1a and di-
methyl malonate 2a were employed as the model substrates to
test our hypothesis. When the reaction of 1a with 2a and CO
2

screened other parameters. First, some common photocatalysts
were tested, and the results indicated that PC4 gave the best
result, affording 3aa in 80% yield (entries 1−4). Additionally,
the solvent also showed an obvious effect. In DMF, 3aa was
obtained in a 67% yield (entry 5). However, the reaction in
NMP and MeCN afforded only 3aa in 45 and 50% yields,
respectively (entries 6 and 7). Common bases were also
screened. Na

14). Finally, control experiments demonstrated that the

2

(entry 15).
Next, we investigated the reaction scope. First, a series of
1,3-enynes smoothly reacted with dimethyl malonate 2a and
CO
2
under the optimized conditions, affording the desired
products with good efficiency (Scheme 2). It was found that
the electronic nature of the substituents at the para position of
the phenyl ring had no obvious effect. Substrates bearing
electron-donating groups, such as Me (1b), Et (1c), OMe
(1e),
t
Bu (1e), and Ph (1f), and the one bearing electron-
withdrawing groups, such as fluoro (1g), chloro (1h), bromo
(1i), cyano (1j), and trifluoromethyl (1k), afforded 3ba−3ka
in 73−80% yields. Additionally, those with m-methyl (1l), m-
chloro (1m), m-bromo (1n), o-methyl (1o), and o-chloro (1p)
all worked well, leading to the desired products 3la−3pa in
58−81% yields, indicating that steric hindrance had no obvious
effect. Furthermore, 2-naphthyl- (1q) and 2-thienyl- (1r)
substituted 1,3-enynes also afforded the desired products 3qa
and 3ra in 82 and 71% yields, respectively. It is noteworthy
that substitutions at the 3 position had a profound influence, as
no desired product 3sa could be detected when 1s was
employed. Delightedly, 1,3-enynes substituted with 3-

only resulted in a messy mixture with trace product detected.
However, the one bearing an estrone motif 1C was amenable
to the reaction conditions, furnishing 3Ca in 34% yield.

scope of malonates could be further expanded to substituted
dimethyl ones. For example, those bearing ethyl (2j), benzyl
(2k), allylic (2l), methyl ester (2m), propargyl (2n), and ester
(2o) were all good reaction candidates to afford the desired
products 3ja−3oa. Notably, the unsaturated bonds of the
dimethyl malonates (2l and 2n) remained intact, providing
opportunities for further derivatization. Additionally, malo-

yielding the desired 2,3-allenoic acids (3ap−3ar).
Then, some essential control experiments were conducted to
investigate the possible reaction mechanism. As shown in
Scheme 4, the reaction of 1a and 2o was conducted with the
addition of an excess of D
2
O (30 equiv). As excepted, the
deuterated product D-3ao was isolated in 49% yield with more
than 95% D at the allenyl position, indicating the generation of
the allenyl carbanion (Scheme 4a). Upon addition of 3 equiv
of TEMPO, the reaction was almost inhibited, with the
detection of the radical adduct IM-A by HRMS (see Figure S4
of the Supporting Information for details), thus consistent with
a radical pathway (Scheme 4b). Particularly, the luminescence
quenching experiments indicated that this reaction was
initiated by reductive quenching of photoexited Ir-

Figure S5 of the Supporting Information for details). Finally, a
light on/off experiment indicated that continuous light
irradiation was essential to the success (see Figure S6 of the
Supporting Information for details).
To demonstrate the utility of this method, a 1 mmol
reaction of 1a with 2a and CO
2
was conducted under the
slightly modified conditions, leading to the desired product 3aa
in 77% yield (Scheme 4c). Then, further transformations of
3aa were also conducted. First, a CuCl-catalyzed annulation of
3aa proceeded smoothly, delivering the cycloaddition product
4 in 76% yield (Scheme 4d). Furthermore, a cyclization
reaction of 3aa catalyzed by PdCl
2
in the presence of allyl
bromide afforded allyl furanone 5 in 70% yield (Scheme 4e).
Treatment of 3aa with N-iodosuccinimide (NIS) furnished
iodo-lactone 6 in 31% yield (Scheme 4f). Additionally, the
amination of 3aa with methyl glycinate hydrochloride led to
amide 7 in 53% yield (Scheme 4g). Alternatively, amination of
3aa with benzylamine, followed by the treatment of the
obtained amide with NIS, afforded iodo-lactam 8 in 51% yield
(Scheme 4h).

In conclusion, we have developed the first visible-light-
promoted 1,4-carbon/carboxylation of 1,3-enynes with malo-
nates and CO
2
, leading to a series of valuable tetrasubstituted
2,3-allenoic acids in good yields. This new methodology
features good functional group tolerance, ease of scale-up, and
facile transformations. Mechanistic investigations indicate that
successive single-electron transfer (SSET) reduction is likely
involved, with the allenoic anion serving as a key intermediate.
